plan: Social science paired passages of about 690 words (CLD-P-ACT-R-000027) on ending library fines. Written after the Reading 200 audit found no item calibrated hard: three items labelled hard rely on cross-passage synthesis and on choices that overstate an author's skepticism or omit a qualification.

passages.title: Ending Library Fines (paired passages)
passages.text:
SOCIAL SCIENCE: Passage A is from an essay by a librarian; Passage B is from an essay by a city budget analyst. Both are original texts written for this practice set.

Passage A

For most of the twentieth century, the overdue fine seemed as natural a part of the public library as the card catalog. A few cents a day, the reasoning went, would remind borrowers that a book belonged to everyone. Over the past decade, however, many library systems in the United States have stopped charging fines, and the results have persuaded a number of librarians that the old reasoning was backward.

The first surprise was who had been paying. When library systems examined their records, they often found that blocked accounts (cards suspended because of unpaid fines) were concentrated in the poorest neighborhoods. A child who owed eight dollars could not check out another book until the debt was paid, and many such children simply stopped coming. The fine had not taught responsibility; it had taught some families that the library was not for them.

The second surprise was what happened to the books. Many systems that ended fines reported that most borrowers continued to return items on time, and several saw long-overdue materials come back as patrons who had stayed away for years returned. Without the embarrassment of an unpayable bill, bringing back a late book became an ordinary errand rather than a confession.

Nor were fines ever a large part of library budgets. In most systems they brought in less than one percent of revenue, and collecting them took staff time at the desk that could have been spent helping readers. Measured against the library's mission, fines were expensive.

Passage B

Advocates of ending library fines have assembled an appealing story, and parts of it are true. Fines do fall hardest on families with the least money, and a suspended card can keep a child away from the library at exactly the age when reading habits form. Any library that blocks children's accounts over a few dollars should rethink that policy.

But the evidence that fine-free policies cause no harm is thinner than the story suggests. Most of the reports come from the libraries themselves, typically comparing a single year before the change with a single year after it. Circulation, staffing, and the local economy all shift from year to year, and a library that has just made a well-publicized change has every reason to emphasize good news. Few systems have tracked what happens to the small share of borrowers who keep popular items for months, and those are precisely the borrowers a fine was meant to influence. When a library owns only three copies of a new bestseller, one patron who keeps a copy for an extra six weeks makes dozens of others wait longer.

Nor is the budget question as simple as it sounds. Fines may amount to less than one percent of a large system's revenue, but in a small rural library the same few thousand dollars may be a meaningful share of the money available for new books. A policy that works in a city of a million people may not transfer to a town of four thousand.

None of this is an argument for keeping fines exactly as they were. It is an argument for measuring carefully before declaring victory, and for designing policies, such as forgiving children's fines while keeping modest charges for adults, that address the real harms without assuming that removing fines costs nothing.

candidates.stem: The main purpose of Passage A is to:

choices.A: argue that ending overdue fines has served libraries and their patrons well.
choices.B: explain how library fines were calculated in the twentieth century.
choices.C: propose forgiving children's fines while keeping charges for adults.
choices.D: show that most library patrons returned books late when fines existed.

candidates.evidence: the results have persuaded a number of librarians that the old reasoning was backward
candidates.explanation: Passage A presents two "surprises" and a budget point, all supporting the claim that ending fines has worked.

B.rationale: The passage mentions "a few cents a day" only in passing.

C.rationale: This compromise is proposed in Passage B, not Passage A.

D.rationale: Passage A makes no such claim.

hints: What does each paragraph of Passage A add to the author's case?

strategy.explanation: Summarize Passage A in one sentence.

candidates.remember: Keep the two passages' claims separate.

candidates.stem: In Passage A, the statement that returning a late book had been "a confession" suggests that, when fines existed, returning an overdue book:

choices.A: was a chance for borrowers to explain why they were late.
choices.B: required borrowers to sign a statement at the desk.
choices.C: felt like admitting a wrong that would bring a penalty.
choices.D: was easier than it became after fines were ended.

candidates.explanation: Paired with "the embarrassment of an unpayable bill," "confession" suggests returning a late book meant admitting fault and facing a penalty.

B.rationale: The word is figurative; no literal statement is described.

D.rationale: The passage says it became easier, "an ordinary errand," after fines ended.

hints: What does the sentence contrast "confession" with?

strategy.explanation: Predict what a confession involves, then match.

candidates.remember: Read figurative words alongside the phrase they are contrasted with.

candidates.stem: The last paragraph of Passage A mainly serves to:

choices.A: show that libraries spent fine revenue on children's programs.
choices.B: answer a likely objection that libraries need the money fines bring in.
choices.C: explain why patrons stopped visiting libraries that charged fines.
choices.D: introduce a new problem that ending fines has created.

candidates.evidence: Nor were fines ever a large part of library budgets.
candidates.explanation: After presenting benefits, the author addresses the obvious counterargument (lost revenue) by noting that fines were a tiny share of revenue and cost staff time to collect.

A.rationale: The paragraph does not say how fine revenue was spent.

C.rationale: That is the subject of the second paragraph.

D.rationale: The paragraph supports ending fines; it raises no new problem.

hints: What objection might a reader raise after paragraphs 2 and 3?

strategy.explanation: Ask what doubt the paragraph puts to rest.

candidates.remember: A paragraph about cost often answers an objection.

candidates.stem: The author of Passage B regards the case made by advocates of ending fines as:

choices.A: entirely mistaken about the effects of fines on poor families.
choices.B: fully proven by the reports libraries have published.
choices.D: partly convincing but resting on evidence weaker than they suggest.

candidates.explanation: Passage B grants that parts of the story are true but says "the evidence that fine-free policies cause no harm is thinner than the story suggests."

A.rationale: Passage B agrees that fines fall hardest on families with the least money.

C.rationale: Passage B says small libraries need separate consideration, not that the case is irrelevant to them.

hints: What does the author of Passage B accept, and what does the author doubt?

strategy.explanation: Rule out choices that are all-or-nothing.

candidates.remember: Attitude answers must match both what an author accepts and what the author doubts.

candidates.stem: According to Passage B, one reason the libraries' own reports may be unreliable is that the reports:

choices.A: were written before any library had actually ended fines.
choices.B: counted only the books returned by children.
choices.C: often compare only one year before the change with one year after it.
choices.D: came from libraries that later restored their fines.

candidates.evidence: typically comparing a single year before the change with a single year after it
candidates.explanation: Passage B notes that the reports typically compare one year before with one year after, while other factors change from year to year.

A.rationale: The reports describe results after the change.

B.rationale: Nothing says the reports counted only children's returns.

D.rationale: The passage says nothing about libraries restoring fines.

hints: Reread the start of Passage B's second paragraph.

strategy.explanation: Find the sentence about how the reports were made.

candidates.remember: Detail questions about one passage stay inside that passage.

candidates.subskill: Points of agreement across paired passages
candidates.stem: Based on the passages, both authors would most likely agree that:

choices.A: fines make up a negligible share of the budget of every public library.
choices.B: fine-free policies have been clearly shown to cause no harm to libraries.
choices.C: libraries should keep modest fines in place for their adult borrowers.
choices.D: overdue fines can keep children from poorer families away from the library.

candidates.evidence: a suspended card can keep a child away from the library
candidates.explanation: Passage A describes children who "simply stopped coming" because of fines, and Passage B agrees that fines "fall hardest on families with the least money" and can keep a child away.

A.rationale: Passage B argues that in small rural libraries fine revenue can matter.

B.rationale: Passage B says this evidence is thin.

hints: What does Passage B concede in its first paragraph?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate any choice one author would reject.

candidates.remember: Agreement answers must be supported by both passages.

author_checklist.hardness: Choice A echoes a statistic both passages mention, but Passage B limits it to large systems; students must notice the qualification.

candidates.subskill: How one author would respond to the other
candidates.stem: The author of Passage B would most likely respond to Passage A's report that "most borrowers continued to return items on time" by:

choices.A: arguing that most borrowers in fact began returning their items late once fines ended.
choices.B: agreeing that it proves fine-free policies cause no harm to libraries at all.
choices.C: accepting it but noting that it ignores the few who keep popular items for months.
choices.D: pointing out that the report applies only to the return of children's books.

candidates.evidence: Few systems have tracked what happens to the small share of borrowers who keep popular items for months
candidates.explanation: Passage B's objection is not that most borrowers return late but that averages hide a small, costly group, so the author would grant the claim and point to what it leaves out.

A.rationale: Passage B does not dispute that most borrowers return items on time.

B.rationale: Passage B says the evidence that such policies cause no harm is thin.

D.rationale: Nothing limits the report to children's books.

hints: Does Passage B ever say most borrowers return items late?

strategy.explanation: Separate disagreement about the claim from disagreement about what it leaves out.

candidates.remember: A response can accept a claim yet say it is incomplete.

author_checklist.hardness: Choice A sounds like the skeptic's view but contradicts it; students must see that Passage B questions what the average conceals, not the average itself.

candidates.subskill: Relating a proposal to the other passage
candidates.stem: Passage B's suggestion of "forgiving children's fines while keeping modest charges for adults" relates to the concerns raised in Passage A in that it:

choices.A: meets Passage A's concern about children but keeps an incentive for adults.
choices.B: rejects Passage A's concern about children as greatly exaggerated.
choices.C: adopts Passage A's view that fines should be removed for every borrower.
choices.D: shows that the budget figures given in Passage A were incorrect.

candidates.evidence: forgiving children's fines while keeping modest charges for adults
candidates.explanation: Passage A's central example is children kept away by fines; Passage B's compromise removes those fines while keeping a modest incentive for adults.

B.rationale: Passage B agrees with that concern.

C.rationale: Passage B would keep modest charges for adults.

D.rationale: The proposal says nothing about Passage A's figures.

hints: Whose fines would the proposal forgive, and why does that matter to Passage A?

strategy.explanation: Compare the proposal with Passage A's second paragraph.

candidates.remember: Cross-passage questions ask how one passage's idea bears on the other's.

withdrawn.reason: withdrawn before review: both blind solvers noted it tests the same idea as R027-08 (a few borrowers who keep popular items burden many), and its key wording ('even if most return on time') nearly gives away R027-08's answer; solver B also rated this hard-labelled item easy. Not resubmitted: R027-08 covers the idea.

item.stem: In Passage B, the example of the library that owns three copies of a new bestseller mainly serves to show that:

choices.A: most borrowers return popular books late when there are no fines.
choices.B: a few borrowers who keep items long can burden many others even if most return on time.
choices.C: libraries should buy more copies of popular books instead of charging fines.
choices.D: fine-free libraries lend fewer books than libraries that charge fines.

item.evidence: one patron who keeps a copy for an extra six weeks makes dozens of others wait longer
item.explanation: The example follows the point about "the small share of borrowers who keep popular items for months": even a single such borrower imposes delays on many others, a cost an average return rate can hide.

A.rationale: Passage B does not dispute that most borrowers return items on time; it focuses on a small share.

C.rationale: The author does not propose buying more copies.

D.rationale: Nothing compares the number of books lent.

hints: Which borrowers does the sentence before the example discuss?

strategy.explanation: Connect the example to the sentence just before it.

item.remember: An example usually illustrates the claim right before it.

author_checklist.hardness: Choice A sounds like the author's skepticism but overstates it: Passage B concedes that most borrowers return items on time and objects only that a small, costly minority goes unmeasured.
